name: Monolith 5x200 Multi-Channel Amplifier
amazonQuery: Monolith 5x200 multi-channel home theater power amplifier
summary: A five-channel Class AB power amp rated at 200 W/ch into 8 Ω with all channels driven, two toroidal transformers and XLR inputs, built for big rooms and hard-to-drive speakers.
verdict:
The Monolith 5x200 takes the five ear-level channels off your receiver and drives them from its own heavyweight supply. Monoprice quotes **200 W/ch into 8 Ω, all channels driven across 20 Hz–20 kHz**, uses **two toroidal transformers** and a **Class AB** output stage, and lists a signal-to-noise ratio above **120 dB**. You need a receiver with pre-outs, such as the [Denon AVR-X3800H](/gear/denon-avr-x3800h/) or [Marantz Cinema 50](/gear/marantz-cinema-50/).

**Show the maths.** Five channels × 200 W = **1,000 W** of rated output with every channel working, which is the rating most receivers never publish. Against the [Outlaw Audio 5000x](/gear/outlaw-audio-5000x/) at 120 W/ch, that is 10 × log10(200 ÷ 120) = **2.2 dB** more headroom per channel. With 85 dB [sensitivity](/glossary/speaker-sensitivity/) speakers, 200 W gives 85 + 23 = **108 dB at 1 m**, and about **97 dB** at a 3.5 m seat after the 10.9 dB distance loss.

**How it fits a 7.1.4 build.** That layout has 7 + 4 = 11 speakers. Put front left, center, right and the two side surrounds on the Monolith; a nine-channel receiver then powers only the remaining six (rear surrounds and four heights).

The trade-offs are size, heat and price: Class AB runs warm, so leave space above it, and per watt it costs more than the Outlaw. Buy it for large rooms and low-sensitivity speakers. See our [best home theater amplifier](/best-home-theater-amplifier/) guide.
bestFor: Large rooms and low-sensitivity speakers that need real all-channel power
skipIf: Your speakers are efficient, your room is medium-sized or your receiver has no pre-outs

faqs.q: Is the Monolith 5x200 rated with all channels driven?
faqs.a: Yes. Monoprice quotes 200 W per channel into 8 ohms with all channels driven across 20 Hz to 20 kHz. That is a tougher test than the two-channels-driven figures most receivers publish.

faqs.q: Monolith 5x200 vs Outlaw Audio 5000x: which should I buy?
faqs.a: The Monolith is rated at 200 W per channel against the Outlaw's 120 W, about 2.2 dB more headroom, and suits large rooms with low-sensitivity speakers. The Outlaw costs much less and is enough for most medium rooms.

faqs.q: How do I connect the Monolith 5x200 to a receiver?
faqs.a: Run RCA or XLR cables from the receiver's pre-outs for front left, center, right and the two surrounds to the amp, then connect those speakers to the amp. The receiver keeps decoding and room correction.

name: Marantz MM7025 Power Amplifier
summary: A two-channel Marantz power amp rated at 140 W/ch into 8 Ω and 170 W/ch into 6 Ω, with XLR and RCA inputs, the tidy way to add the eleventh and twelfth channels to a nine-channel receiver.
verdict:
The MM7025 is a **two-channel power amplifier**, and its natural job is completing a big Atmos layout. A 7.1.4 system has 7 + 4 = **11** speakers. A nine-channel receiver like the [Denon AVR-X3800H](/gear/denon-avr-x3800h/) or [Marantz Cinema 50](/gear/marantz-cinema-50/) powers nine, and the MM7025 drives the other two from its own supply, usually the front left and right.

Marantz rates it at **140 W/ch into 8 Ω and 170 W/ch into 6 Ω**, with Marantz's stated conditions of 20 Hz–20 kHz and two channels driven, an **oversized EI-core power transformer**, discrete output transistors and Marantz's current-feedback design. Each channel takes **balanced XLR or RCA**.

**Show the maths.** Against a receiver channel rated at 105 W, 10 × log10(140 ÷ 105) = **1.25 dB** more headroom on paper. That alone is small. The real gain is that the receiver's supply now feeds nine channels instead of eleven, so it has more in reserve on loud scenes. With 86 dB [sensitivity](/glossary/speaker-sensitivity/) towers, 140 W gives 86 + 21.5 = **107.5 dB at 1 m** and about **96.5 dB** at a 3.5 m seat. Set a proper [crossover](/glossary/crossover/) so the subwoofer handles everything below 80 Hz and the fronts keep their headroom for the midrange.

Auto-standby and remote power control mean it can wake with the system. If you need five or seven channels, the [Outlaw Audio 5000x](/gear/outlaw-audio-5000x/) or [Outlaw Audio 7000x](/gear/outlaw-audio-7000x/) gives more channels per dollar. See the [best home theater amplifier](/best-home-theater-amplifier/) guide.

faqs.q: Can I use the Marantz MM7025 with an AV receiver?
faqs.a: Yes, if the receiver has pre-outs. Connect the pre-outs for the two channels you want to offload, usually front left and right, to the MM7025 and the speakers to the amp. The receiver still handles decoding and room correction.

faqs.q: Is the MM7025 worth it over my receiver's own amps?
faqs.a: Mainly for big systems. Going from 105 W to 140 W adds only about 1.25 dB, but moving two channels to a separate supply leaves the receiver with fewer channels to feed on loud scenes.

name: Outlaw Audio 7000x
summary: A seven-channel power amp rated at 130 W/ch into 8 Ω and 200 W/ch into 4 Ω with all channels driven, plus XLR inputs, a 12 V trigger and a five-year warranty.
verdict:
The 7000x gives you **seven channels of external amplification**, enough to take every ear-level speaker in a 7.1 or 7.1.4 system off your receiver. Outlaw rates it at **130 W/ch into 8 Ω and 200 W/ch into 4 Ω, all channels driven, 20 Hz–20 kHz, under 0.03% THD**. Each channel has its own power-supply rectification and protection relay, and a **12 V trigger** switches it on with your receiver.

**Show the maths.** Seven channels × 130 W = **910 W** of rated output with everything working. Most receivers quote power with two channels driven, so a 105 W receiver rating does not mean 105 W on seven channels at once. Per channel, 10 × log10(130 ÷ 105) is only about **0.9 dB**; the bigger win is that the receiver's supply now powers just the heights.

Room check: with 87 dB [sensitivity](/glossary/speaker-sensitivity/) speakers, 130 W gives 87 + 21.1 = **108 dB at 1 m** and about **98.5 dB** at a 3 m seat, enough for most medium and large living rooms. If your speakers dip to 4 Ω ([impedance](/glossary/impedance/) explained), the 200 W rating gives another 1.9 dB.

You need a receiver with pre-outs for each channel, such as the [Denon AVR-X3800H](/gear/denon-avr-x3800h/). Against the [Monolith 5x200](/gear/monolith-5x200/), you trade 1.9 dB per channel for two extra channels and a lower price. See our [best home theater amplifier](/best-home-theater-amplifier/) picks.

faqs.q: Outlaw Audio 7000x vs Monolith 5x200: which is better?
faqs.a: The Monolith is rated at 200 W per channel against 130 W, about 1.9 dB more headroom, but has five channels. The Outlaw powers seven channels for less money and is enough for most medium and large rooms.

faqs.q: Does the Outlaw 7000x work with any receiver?
faqs.a: Only with receivers that have pre-outs for the channels you want it to drive. Many 7.2 receivers only have subwoofer and zone outputs, so check the back panel before you buy.

faqs.q: Will the 7000x turn on with my receiver?
faqs.a: Yes, if your receiver has a 12 V trigger output. Connect it to the amp's trigger input and the 7000x powers on and off with the receiver.

name: Outlaw Audio 5000x
summary: A five-channel power amp rated at 120 W/ch into 8 Ω and 180 W/ch into 4 Ω, with XLR and RCA inputs and a 12 V trigger, the value way to power a full 5.1 front stage and surrounds.
verdict:
The 5000x powers the five speakers that carry most of a movie: **front left, center, right and two surrounds**. Outlaw rates it at **120 W/ch into 8 Ω and 180 W/ch into 4 Ω, 20 Hz–20 kHz, under 0.02% THD**. Inputs are **balanced XLR** and hum-rejecting RCA, a **12 V trigger** wakes it with your receiver, and each channel has its own rectification and protection relay.

**Show the maths.** Loudness at 1 m = sensitivity + 10 × log10(watts). With an 88 dB [sensitivity](/glossary/speaker-sensitivity/) center, 120 W gives 88 + 20.8 = **108.8 dB at 1 m** and about **99 dB** at a 3 m seat. Against a receiver channel rated at 80 W, that is 10 × log10(120 ÷ 80) = **1.8 dB** more headroom, and the 4 Ω rating adds another 1.8 dB for speakers with low [impedance](/glossary/impedance/).

**Where it fits.** In a 5.1.4 or 7.1.4 build, the 5000x takes the five ear-level mains and the receiver keeps only the heights (and rear surrounds in 7.1.4). That halves the load on the receiver's supply. You need pre-outs for all five channels; nine-channel models like the [Denon AVR-X3800H](/gear/denon-avr-x3800h/) have them.

If you want all seven ear-level channels covered, step up to the [Outlaw Audio 7000x](/gear/outlaw-audio-7000x/). If your room is large and your speakers are inefficient, the [Monolith 5x200](/gear/monolith-5x200/) adds 2.2 dB per channel. See the [best home theater amplifier](/best-home-theater-amplifier/) guide.

name: Yamaha A-S501 Integrated Amplifier
summary: An 85 W/ch stereo integrated amp with a built-in DAC, phono stage and subwoofer output, a good base for a 2.1 TV and music system.
verdict:
The A-S501 is a **stereo integrated amplifier**, not a surround receiver. It makes sense in a 2.0 or 2.1 setup where music matters as much as movies, with the TV feeding it over optical.

Yamaha rates it at **85 W/ch (8 Ω, 20 Hz–20 kHz, 0.019% THD)**. Compare that with the [Denon PMA-600NE](/gear/denon-pma-600ne/) at 45 W/ch into 8 Ω: 10 × log10(85 ÷ 45) = **2.8 dB** more headroom. That is close to the 3 dB you get from doubling power, and it is audible with less sensitive bookshelf speakers.

Room maths: with 87 dB [sensitivity](/glossary/speaker-sensitivity/) speakers, 85 W gives 87 + 19.3 = about 106 dB at 1 m, or about 97 dB at a 3 m seat. That covers loud movie nights in a living room, especially if the **subwoofer output** sends bass to a powered sub. A sub such as the [SVS SB-1000 Pro](/gear/svs-sb-1000-pro/) takes the deepest notes off the amp entirely and lets the speakers play louder cleanly.

The built-in DAC (optical and coaxial) and MM phono stage make it a tidy hub for a TV, turntable and streamer. What you give up is surround: no center channel, no surrounds, no Atmos. If you want those, start with our [best home theater receiver](/best-home-theater-receiver/) guide instead.

name: Denon PMA-600NE Integrated Amplifier
summary: A stereo integrated amp with Bluetooth, a built-in DAC and a phono stage, rated at 45 W/ch into 8 Ω and best matched with efficient speakers in a small room.
verdict:
The PMA-600NE is a **stereo integrated amplifier** for a 2.0 or 2.1 TV and music system. It connects to the TV over optical or coaxial, streams from your phone over Bluetooth and has a moving-magnet phono stage.

Denon rates it at **45 W/ch into 8 Ω** and **70 W/ch into 4 Ω**. Here is what that means. Loudness at 1 m = sensitivity + 10 × log10(watts), and 10 × log10(45) is 16.5 dB. With 87 dB [sensitivity](/glossary/speaker-sensitivity/) speakers, that is about 103.5 dB at 1 m and roughly 94 dB at a 3 m seat. With efficient 90 dB speakers, you gain 3 dB, the same as doubling the amp's power.

That is the key buying lesson: **choose efficient speakers** with this amp. Against the [Yamaha A-S501](/gear/yamaha-a-s501/) at 85 W/ch, the Denon gives up 10 × log10(85 ÷ 45) = **2.8 dB**. A speaker that is 3 dB more sensitive closes that gap completely. Note that 4 Ω speakers draw more current; check your speakers' [impedance](/glossary/impedance/) before you assume the 70 W figure applies.

Analog Mode switches off the digital circuits for cleaner analog playback. It is a strong choice for a small room. For surround sound, see our [best budget home theater receiver](/best-budget-home-theater-receiver/) guide.

faqs.q: Is the Denon PMA-600NE powerful enough?
faqs.a: With efficient speakers in a small or medium room, yes. With 87 dB speakers, 45 W gives about 103.5 dB at 1 m and roughly 94 dB at 3 m. Low-sensitivity speakers or larger rooms call for more power.

faqs.q: Can the Denon PMA-600NE connect to a TV?
faqs.a: Yes. Use the TV's optical output into one of the amp's digital inputs. It plays stereo only, so surround tracks are downmixed by the TV.

name: Fosi Audio V3 Amplifier
summary: A tiny, low-cost Class D stereo amp built on the TI TPA3255 chip, good for powering passive speakers on a budget but bare on inputs and features.
verdict:
The Fosi V3 is a compact **Class D stereo amplifier** built around Texas Instruments' TPA3255 chip and powered by an external DC supply. It is a no-frills way to drive a pair of passive bookshelf speakers from a TV, streamer or DAC.

We have not listed a single power figure because Class D amps like this deliver different output depending on the supply voltage and speaker [impedance](/glossary/impedance/), and marketing numbers are often peak figures. Instead, do the maths for your room. Loudness at 1 m = sensitivity + 10 × log10(watts), and you lose about 9.5 dB by a 3 m seat. To hit 100 dB peaks at 3 m with 86 dB speakers, you need 86 + 10 × log10(P) − 9.5 = 100, so P is about **224 W**. With 90 dB speakers, the same target needs only about **89 W**.

That 4 dB of [sensitivity](/glossary/speaker-sensitivity/) cuts the power needed by more than half, which is why efficient speakers suit a compact amp. For everyday TV listening around 85 dB at the seat, the same 86 dB speakers need under 10 W.

What you give up: there is no digital input, so the TV needs an analog output or a separate DAC, and there is no subwoofer output. For a TV system with more connections, the [Yamaha A-S501](/gear/yamaha-a-s501/) is a big step up. See the [best home theater amplifier](/best-home-theater-amplifier/) guide.

faqs.q: Can the Fosi Audio V3 power home theater speakers?
faqs.a: It can power a pair of passive speakers for stereo TV sound. It has no surround decoding, no digital input and no sub output, so pair it with a TV that has an analog output or use an external DAC.

faqs.q: How much power do I really need?
faqs.a: With 90 dB speakers, about 89 W reaches 100 dB peaks at 3 m; with 86 dB speakers you need about 224 W. Everyday TV listening at around 85 dB needs under 10 W.
